Warm-up: One place each that has changed. Do not let it become a list of restaurants.
Say now that they will write a short report of changes at the end.
Vocabulary: Half of them describe a place, half are have phrases. Drill the have phrases aloud.
Read the completed sentences aloud after the check.
Grammar: Recommending phrases first, then the language of change. Keep them apart on the board.
'I recommend you to try' and 'Have you thought to try' — the two errors of the level.
Practice: Every item is one turn. Make them say both halves aloud.
Task 4 puts the passive and articles from Lessons 28 and 29 back to work.
The model: Structure first, then the phrases, then the balance. They write one afterwards.
Point out the paragraph that starts On the other hand. Without it the report is an advert.
Now you: Asking for a recommendation well is a skill too. Make them do both.
Collect the reports. Do not correct during the writing.
Wrap: Say aloud that the passive and articles came back today.
The Unit 10 Test. Tell them it is retakeable.

Stage 3 · Language

Recommending, and saying what is different

Two sets of phrases. One for the conversation, one for the page.

Read these four recommendations.
  • You could try learning flamenco.
  • If you like skiing, I’d strongly recommend Portillo.
  • Have you thought of trying a traditional Japanese inn?
  • You just have to go to the Charles Bridge.
Which is the strongest, and which leaves the most room to say no?
A recommendation without a reason is just an opinion. A change without a baseline is just a fact.

This lesson brings together two strands that look separate but share one weakness when learners produce them: both need a second half that is easy to forget. A recommendation needs a reason; a description of change needs a comparison point.

Recommendations in English are graded, and the grading is heard. You could try… is tentative and puts no pressure on the listener. I’d recommend… is neutral and states that you hold a view. I’d strongly recommend… and You just have to… are strong, and are only appropriate when you know the person or the subject well. Choosing a level that does not match your relationship with the listener is a real, if quiet, social error.

Alongside these sits the hypothetical formula If I were you, I’d…, which you met in Lesson 23. It works as advice precisely because both speakers know you are not them, so the recommendation is offered rather than imposed.

Describing change requires you to make the ‘before’ explicit. The district has changed tells your reader nothing they can picture. The area used to be run-down, but now it’s full of boutique hotels gives them two states to compare. English supplies three tools for this: the used to…, but now… pattern, quantifying expressions (there has been a sharp increase in…), and explicit comparison (compared with twenty years ago…). A report of changes normally sits mainly in the present perfect and the past simple.

Before you look at the table: the tables below grade the recommendation phrases from tentative to strong, then give the change vocabulary. Note which of them are followed by -ing.
Recommending — from softest to strongest
StrengthPhraseFollowed by

normalI’d recommend… · It’s well worth…a noun, or -ing
strongI’d strongly recommend… · If I were you, I’d…a noun, or a plain verb after I’d
strongestYou just have to… · It’s a real must-see.a plain verb
askingWhere would you recommend I stay? · Is there anything we shouldn’t miss?—

Describing change — on the page
The moveWhat you write
Then and nowIt used to be…, but now… · Ten years ago it was…
The size of the changeThere has been a big increase in… · …have roughly tripled · …fell dramatically

Match the strength to the relationship. You could try… to somebody you barely know; You just have to go… to a friend. Getting this wrong is the most common problem, not the grammar.

Two of these take -ing. You could try learning flamenco. Have you thought of trying a ryokan? Not try to learn in this meaning, and never thought to try.

The mistake to avoid. Not I recommend you to try it but I recommend trying it or I recommend that you try it. Recommend does not take somebody to do.

A report of change needs a turn. Without On the other hand, a description of an improved district reads like an advertisement. One paragraph naming who lost is what makes the rest believable.

Full grammar reference — recommending, and describing change

What it is

Two functional strands. The recommendation set ranges from tentative suggestion (You could try…) to strong endorsement (It’s well worth…) and includes the standard advice formula If I were you, I’d…. The change set is the language of before-and-after: it used to be…, but now…, there’s been a big increase in…, compared with…

What it means, and what it does

Both strands do the same underlying job: they position the listener in relation to a choice or a timeline. A recommendation without a reason is an opinion; a description of change without a comparison point is just a list of facts. The phrases in this lesson supply the missing half — the justification for a recommendation, the baseline for a change.

When and why we use it

This lesson brings together two strands that look separate but share one weakness when learners produce them: both need a second half that is easy to forget. A recommendation needs a reason; a description of change needs a comparison point.

Recommendations in English are graded, and the grading is heard. You could try… is tentative and puts no pressure on the listener. I’d recommend… is neutral and states that you hold a view. I’d strongly recommend… and You just have to… are strong, and are only appropriate when you know the person or the subject well. Choosing a level that does not match your relationship with the listener is a real, if quiet, social error.

Alongside these sits the hypothetical formula If I were you, I’d…, which you met in Lesson 23. It works as advice precisely because both speakers know you are not them, so the recommendation is offered rather than imposed.

Describing change requires you to make the ‘before’ explicit. The district has changed tells your reader nothing they can picture. The area used to be run-down, but now it’s full of boutique hotels gives them two states to compare. English supplies three tools for this: the used to…, but now… pattern, quantifying expressions (there has been a sharp increase in…), and explicit comparison (compared with twenty years ago…). A report of changes normally sits mainly in the present perfect and the past simple.

Typical situations

You need this for giving travel and leisure advice, recommending a service or an activity, and for writing any report that describes how a place, a market or a set of figures has changed over time.

  • Tentative suggestion — You could try…, Have you thought of…?You could try learning flamenco — I made a lot of friends that way.
  • Strong recommendation — I’d strongly recommend…, It’s well worth…I’d strongly recommend Portillo if you like skiing.
  • Advice as a hypothetical — the second conditional formula from Lesson 23.If I were you, I’d stay in a traditional inn.
  • The unmissable thing — You just have to…, Don’t miss…You just have to go to the Charles Bridge at night.
  • Accepting a recommendation — the standard replies.That sounds fabulous. I’ll definitely try it. · OK, I’ll give it a go.
  • Describing a change over time — used to…, but now…The area used to be run-down, but now it’s full of boutique hotels.
  • Quantifying a change — there’s been a big increase / a sharp fall in…There’s been a big increase in the number of visitors.
  • Comparing two points in time — compared with…, whereas…Compared with twenty years ago, the skyline is unrecognisable.

How it differs from similar structures

You could try… (tentative, no pressure) · I’d recommend… (neutral, you have an opinion) · You just have to… (strong, almost an instruction). Match the strength to how well you know the person.
try + -ing = experiment with a method · try + to = attempt something hard. Try learning flamenco (give it a go) vs Try to learn flamenco (it will be difficult).

How to build it

Suggest: You could try + verb-ing  ·  Have you thought of + verb-ing?
Recommend: I’d recommend + verb-ing / noun  ·  It’s well worth + verb-ing
Advise: If I were you, I’d + base verb
Describe change: It used to be + adjective, but now + clause  ·  There has been a + adjective + increase / fall in + noun
TentativeYou could try… · Have you thought of…? · Why don’t you…?
NeutralI’d recommend… · Where would you recommend I stay?
StrongI’d strongly recommend… · It’s well worth… · It’s a must-see.
AdviceIf I were you, I’d… — fixed; the pronouns never change.
AcceptingI’ll give it a go. · That’s a good idea. · I’ll definitely try it.
DecliningThat’s a good idea, but… · Could you recommend something a bit gentler?
Change — then and nowIt used to be…, but now it’s… · It has changed dramatically.
Change — quantitya sharp / slight / dramatic increase in… · a steady fall in…
Change — contrastCompared with… · whereas… · on the other hand…

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Recommend does not take somebody to do something in standard English. Say I’d recommend staying there or I recommend that you stay there, never I recommend you to stay.
  • Worth, try (= experiment with) and think of are all followed by -ing. Try to + base verb means something different: attempt something difficult.
  • Where would you recommend I stay? keeps statement word order after recommend — it is an embedded question (Lesson 12).
  • Increase and decrease are both nouns and verbs, with different stress: the noun is IN-crease, the verb is in-CREASE.
  • Use compared with or compared to — both are accepted — but keep the two things genuinely comparable: compared with twenty years ago, not compared with the past skyline was different.
  • A report of changes is normally written mostly in the present perfect (what has happened up to now) and the past simple (what it used to be like). Mixing in the present continuous makes it read as a live commentary.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I recommend you to visit the castle. → I’d recommend visiting the castle.Recommend does not take somebody to do.
  • It’s well worth to see at night. → It’s well worth seeing at night.Worth takes -ing.
  • Have you thought of to stay in a ryokan? → Have you thought of staying in a ryokan?After a preposition, -ing.
  • Where would you recommend do I stay? → Where would you recommend I stay?Embedded questions keep statement word order.
  • If I was you, I’d book early. → If I were you, I’d book early.The advice formula is fixed with were.
  • There has been a big increase of visitors. → There has been a big increase in visitors.Increase takes in, not of.

More examples in context

  • tentativeYou could try learning flamenco — there are some fantastic schools.
  • suggestion as a questionHave you thought of staying in a traditional Japanese inn?
  • strongIf you like skiing, I’d strongly recommend Portillo or Valle Nevado.
  • must-doYou just have to go up to the castle, especially at night.
  • adviceIf I were you, I’d book the ferry before you arrive.
  • acceptingThat sounds fabulous. I’ll definitely try it.
  • asking for an alternativeThat’s a good idea, but my knees are bad. Could you recommend something a bit gentler?
  • change, then and nowThe run-down warehouses used to be empty; now they’re galleries and trendy cafés.
  • change, quantifiedThere has been a dramatic increase in the number of visitors over the past decade.
  • change, comparedCompared with twenty years ago, the skyline is dominated by skyscrapers.

A tip for remembering it

Attach a reason to every recommendation and a baseline to every change. I’d recommend the ryokan → add because you get the food and the baths included. The district has changed → add compared with twenty years ago. Without the second half, neither sentence gives your listener anything to act on.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Grade your recommendation: You could try… → I’d recommend… → You just have to…
  2. Recommend, worth, try (= experiment) and think of all take -ing.
  3. Never say recommend somebody to do something.
  4. If I were you, I’d… is a fixed advice formula.
  5. Describe change with used to…, but now… and there has been an increase / fall in…
  6. Give every recommendation a reason and every change a comparison point.

Stage 5 · Main input

A report of what changed

Read it as a writer. You are going to write one like it.

Before you read: what makes a description of an improved district believable?

Choose one. The model does three of these and deliberately avoids one.

The old port district: then and now

Ten years ago the port district was run-down and more or less empty after six o’clock. The warehouses had been closed since the 1990s, the streets were badly lit, and an open-air cinema down there would have been unheard of.

It is a different place now. Most of the warehouses have been renovated. Two of them are hotels, one is a nightclub, and the largest is used as a market that stays open until midnight. There has been a big increase in the number of visitors: the city counted 40,000 in 2016 and just under 300,000 last year. The district has become a destination rather than somewhere people drove through.

The skyline has changed too. Three towers were built between 2019 and 2022, which is what most people notice first, although it is the small things — lighting, benches, a bus route — that actually brought people back.

On the other hand, not everybody has gained. Compared with ten years ago, rents in the district have roughly tripled, and most of the families who lived there have moved further out. The cafés are trendy and the residents are new.

It used to be a place where people worked. Now it is a place people visit. Whether that counts as an improvement depends entirely on which of the two groups you belong to.

What the model does, in five moves
  • Starts with what it used to be like, so the change has something to be measured against.
  • Gives two real numbers, and a date range for the towers.
  • Separates what people notice from what actually worked — towers versus bus routes.
  • Turns at On the other hand and names who lost. This is what makes the rest believable.
  • Refuses the easy verdict. It depends on which group you are in — and the report says so.

Your plan
